answer.text: ΔE = 13.6(1/20² − 1/21²) eV = 0.00316 eV, so f ≈ 7.64 × 10¹¹ Hz. With T₂₀ ≈ 1.21 × 10⁻¹² s, T₂₀f ≈ 0.93, approaching 1 for large n. This is the correspondence between the photon frequency and classical orbital frequency. The source’s numerical working is inconsistent.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w3:a.hint: Combine the allowed angular momentum with the orbit or energy relation given in the question.
notes: In the Bohr model, mvr = nℏ and Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force. These give r_n proportional to n² and energy proportional to −1/n².
For an orbital period, use 2πr/v. A photon from a transition uses the level-energy difference; its frequency is not generally the classical orbit frequency.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w3:c.i.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.

sup-c03b382682d3b785-54w3:c.iii.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.
notes: Changing flux can drive induced current. Its magnetic effect opposes that flux change, transferring mechanical energy into electrical heating.
Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.
